## 1. Project Overview

The goal of this assignment is to practice collecting data from a web API and organizing it with R. I selected the New York Times Books API to explore the Hardcover Fiction bestseller list.

I have already downloaded a sample of 15 books and stored the results in JSON, CSV, and SQLite formats. This **Approach** shows the data source, loading process, database structure, basic cleaning checks, and a small preliminary review. The full exploratory analysis will be completed in the Code Base.

## 2. Research Questions

I will investigate these questions:

1.  What are the top five bestselling hardcover fiction books, and what is each book's rank?
2.  Which authors appear on the bestseller list?
3.  How many weeks have the top five books been on the list?

The bestseller **rank** is the book's position on this list. It is not a measure of the number of copies sold.

## 3. Data Source and API Endpoint

**Source:** [New York Times Books API](https://developer.nytimes.com/docs/books-product/1/overview)

**Endpoint:**

`https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json`

- HTTP method: `GET`
- Query parameter: `api-key`
- Response format: JSON
- Selected list: Hardcover Fiction
- Authentication: API key stored privately as `NYT_API_KEY` in `~/.Renviron`

The endpoint returns the latest available list. The saved sample used in this Approach has a **print publication date of November 8, 2026**. The print date can be later than the web release date. Results may change when the API is called again.

## 4. API Connection and JSON Download

I created an API application and saved my key in an R environment variable. The actual request is performed in `fetch_nyt_books.R`, which saves the original JSON and creates the cleaned CSV and SQLite records.

The following is the main request code. It is shown for documentation and is **not re-run during rendering**, so this report uses the same saved sample each time.

```{r api-request-example, eval=FALSE}
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)

api_key <- Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY")
stopifnot(nzchar(api_key))

endpoint <- paste0(
  "https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/",
  "lists/current/hardcover-fiction.json"
)

response <- httr::GET(
  endpoint,
  query = list("api-key" = api_key),
  httr::timeout(30)
)
httr::stop_for_status(response)

raw_json <- httr::content(
  response,
  as = "text",
  encoding = "UTF-8"
)

# The complete fetch_nyt_books.R script validates the response,
# loads SQLite, and saves the original JSON and tidy CSV.
```

The original response is saved as `data/nyt_hardcover_fiction_raw.json`. I do not include my API key or secret in the submission.

## 5. Load JSON, Create the Database, and Verify the Tables

I used `jsonlite` to load the downloaded JSON file. Then I used `DBI` and `RSQLite` to create a local database and verify the data. The SQL statements below create the tables if necessary; existing records are not deleted.

```{r load-data}
library(jsonlite)
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(knitr)

nyt_json <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  "data/nyt_hardcover_fiction_raw.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)
json_books <- nyt_json$results$books

data.frame(
  List = as.character(nyt_json$results$list_name),
  Print_Date = as.character(nyt_json$results$published_date),
  Books = length(json_books)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Books Downloaded from JSON")
```

This is how the two database tables are created in the actual project:

```{r create-database}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/nyt_books.sqlite"
)
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bestseller_books (
  list_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  published_date TEXT NOT NULL,
  rank INTEGER NOT NULL,
  rank_last_week INTEGER,
  weeks_on_list INTEGER,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  author TEXT,
  publisher TEXT,
  primary_isbn13 TEXT,
  fetched_at_utc TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (list_name, published_date, rank)
)")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS download_log (
  fetched_at_utc TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  endpoint TEXT NOT NULL,
  list_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  published_date TEXT,
  records INTEGER NOT NULL
)")
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Table = DBI::dbListTables(con)),
  caption = "Database Tables"
)
```

The downloader `fetch_nyt_books.R` already inserted the downloaded records. The query below shows them directly from SQLite:

```{r verify-database}
database_books <- DBI::dbGetQuery(
  con,
  "SELECT list_name, published_date, rank, title, author,
          weeks_on_list, rank_last_week, publisher
   FROM bestseller_books
   ORDER BY rank"
)
database_count <- nrow(database_books)
json_count <- length(json_books)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(Source = c("JSON response", "SQLite database"),
             Records = c(json_count, database_count)),
  caption = "JSON and SQLite Record Counts"
)
knitr::kable(
  head(database_books[, c("rank", "title", "author", "weeks_on_list")]),
  caption = "First Six Records Loaded in SQLite"
)
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

## 6. Data Cleaning and Quality Review

The API returns nested JSON. I converted selected fields into a tidy data frame. Each row represents one book, with columns for rank, title, author, and weeks on the list.

```{r cleaning}
get_text <- function(x) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_character_)
  }
  as.character(x[[1]])
}

get_number <- function(x) {
  suppressWarnings(as.integer(get_text(x)))
}

books_clean <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(json_books, function(book) {
    data.frame(
      rank = get_number(book$rank),
      title = get_text(book$title),
      author = get_text(book$author),
      weeks_on_list = get_number(book$weeks_on_list),
      rank_last_week = get_number(book$rank_last_week),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(rank)

quality_check <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Books", "Missing cells", "Duplicate ranks",
            "Invalid ranks", "Negative weeks",
            "JSON / database row counts match"),
  Result = c(
    nrow(books_clean),
    sum(is.na(books_clean)),
    sum(duplicated(books_clean$rank)),
    sum(is.na(books_clean$rank) | books_clean$rank < 1),
    sum(books_clean$weeks_on_list < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    as.character(nrow(books_clean) == database_count)
  )
)

knitr::kable(quality_check, caption = "Preliminary Data Quality Checks")
```

I checked missing values, duplicate ranks, invalid ranks, and negative week counts. I will explain any issues found before the final analysis. The field `rank_last_week` can require special attention because a new book may not have a previous-week rank.

## 7. Preliminary Answers to the Research Questions

This is a **small first look**, not the final analysis. The full Code Base will include more interpretation and any additional charts.

**Question 1: What are the top five books and their rankings?**

```{r top-five}
top_five <- books_clean |>
  dplyr::arrange(rank) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 5) |>
  dplyr::select(rank, title, author, weeks_on_list)

knitr::kable(
  top_five,
  caption = "Five Highest-Ranked Books (Saved API Sample)"
)
```

**Question 2: Which authors appear on the list?**

```{r authors-preview}
author_counts <- books_clean |>
  dplyr::count(author, name = "books_on_list", sort = TRUE)

knitr::kable(
  author_counts,
  caption = "Authors and Number of Books on the List"
)
```

**Question 3: How many weeks have the top books been on the list?**

The `weeks_on_list` column in the table above answers this question. A higher number means that the book has appeared on the list for more weeks; it does not measure total sales.
